title: Places and journeys
job: A trip told in full, with directions inside it
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: DETERMINATE AGAINST INDETERMINATE. idtí and khodít' are two IMPERFECTIVE verbs for one English go on foot; yékhat' and yézdit' are the same pair for going by transport. The split is neither tense nor aspect. The DETERMINATE (idú, yédu) is one trip, in one direction, under way now. The INDETERMINATE (khozhú, yézzhu) is the repeated trip, the habit, the ability, the there-and-back. Sevódnya ya yédu v Moskvú is today's journey; Ya yézzhu v Moskvú kázhdyy god is what I do every year.

THE INDETERMINATE PAST IS A RETURN TRIP, and this is the fact that decides whether you are understood. Vcherá ya khodíl v magazín says I went to the shop AND CAME BACK — one completed there-and-back. Vcherá ya poshyól v magazín says I set off for the shop, and leaves you standing in it. Say the second when you mean the first and the listener will ask when you are coming home.

English go is one verb. Russian forks it TWICE — once by how you travel (idtí on foot against yékhat' by vehicle), and once by the shape of the trip (one direction against there-and-back) — and neither fork exists in English at all. That is why this takes a module rather than a rule: there is no English distinction to hang either half on, so both have to be learnt as facts about the world Russian describes.

The prefixes are already yours from L3-M10 — u- away, vy- out, za- in passing, pri- arrived — and here is what they were doing: A PREFIX ON THE DETERMINATE STEM MAKES A PERFECTIVE. poyékhal, priyékhal, ushyól and prishyól are all built that way, which is why L3-M10's accounts could move forward on exactly those words. The list you memorised was a system all along.

Giving directions re-uses L2-M4 whole and costs nothing new: do plus the genitive for as far as, nalévo, naprávo and pryámo for the turns, ostanóvka and stántsiya for the stops. Only the verbs are new — doyédete for riding as far as somewhere, peresést' for changing lines — and the frame around them has not moved since L2.

sentences.display: Ya yézzhu v Moskvú kázhdyy god.
sentences.script: Я езжу в Москву каждый год.
sentences.cue: I go to Moscow every year.
sentences.literal: I travel-about in Moscow every year.

words.cue: I go, I travel (by transport, habitually)
words.note: The indeterminate present of yézdit': the trip you make over and over, there and back each time. L2-M4's yédu is the single journey happening now.
Every. L1-M4 taught kázhdyy den' as one frozen phrase; the bare adjective, free to take any period, opens here — kázhdyy god, every year.
Year. The accusative of time (kázhdyy god) looks exactly like the dictionary form; góda is the genitive you will meet on dates.

sentences.trap: English every year gives no hint that the verb must change. In Russian the adverb and the verb have to agree about the shape of the trip: a repeated journey takes the indeterminate, whatever else is in the sentence.
sentences.sound: YEZH-zhu — the zhzh is one long buzzing zh, held twice as long as a single one.

variations.changed: there instead of the named place

variations.display: On yézdit v Moskvú kázhdyy god.
variations.script: Он ездит в Москву каждый год.
variations.cue: He goes to Moscow every year.
variations.changed: the third person of the same indeterminate verb

mistake.display: Ya yédu v Moskvú kázhdyy god.
mistake.script: Я еду в Москву каждый год.
mistake.why: yédu is the trip you are on at this moment, so the sentence says I am on my way to Moscow every year — a journey that never ends. A yearly habit takes yézzhu.

sentences.usage: Saying what you do regularly, in answer to how often do you go?
sentences.mnemonic: Repeated means indeterminate: yézzhu goes and comes back, over and over.

words.note: The accusative of L1-M1's Moskvá, which is the case v takes for motion INTO a place. L1-M1's Moskvé is the prepositional, for being there.

sentences.trap: Both English go and Russian yédu can mean I am going now, but only Russian forces the choice. Sevódnya makes it one trip in one direction, so nothing but the determinate will do.
sentences.sound: YE-du — front-stressed, two clean syllables, quite unlike the buzzing yézzhu.

variations.changed: the destination replaced by there
L2-M4's na rabótu, and by transport rather than on foot

mistake.why: yézzhu says this is something you do repeatedly, which sevódnya immediately contradicts. One trip, today, in one direction, is yédu.

sentences.usage: Telling someone what your day looks like.
sentences.mnemonic: One trip, one direction, right now — the determinate yédu, and nothing else.

sentences.cue: Yesterday I went to the shop and came back.

words.cue: to go (on foot, habitually or there-and-back)
words.note: The indeterminate of idtí. Its past — khodíl and khodíla — is L3-M10's, taught there inside the ránshe frame, and in the past it means went AND came back.

sentences.trap: English yesterday I went to the shop says nothing about coming home; Russian's choice of verb says it outright. khodíl closes the loop, and a listener hears the return in the word itself.
sentences.sound: kha-DYIL — stress on the second syllable, and the kh is the scraped h of Scottish loch.

variations.cue: Yesterday he went to the shop and came back.
variations.changed: the third person, same return trip

variations.cue: Yesterday she went to the café and came back.
variations.changed: a woman, so the past takes -a

mistake.why: Correct Russian, and it leaves you in the shop. poshyól is the setting-off, with no return in it — say it about yesterday and the natural next question is when you are coming home.

sentences.usage: Accounting for where you were, when you are plainly back.
sentences.mnemonic: khodíl draws a circle; poshyól draws an arrow.

sentences.display: Ya khozhú na rabótu peshkóm kázhdyy den'.
sentences.script: Я хожу на работу пешком каждый день.
sentences.cue: I walk to work every day.
sentences.literal: I go-about to work on-foot every day.

words.note: The indeterminate present of khodít'. The d of khodít' turns into zh in the ya form only — khozhú but khódit — which is a change worth expecting elsewhere too.

sentences.trap: English needs walk to keep foot travel apart from riding; Russian has it in the verb already. khozhú is on foot by definition, and peshkóm merely says it twice.
sentences.sound: kha-ZHU — stress on the second syllable, and the zh is single here, not the long one of yézzhu.

variations.changed: the destination replaced by there
the third person, where the d comes back

mistake.display: Ya idú na rabótu peshkóm kázhdyy den'.
mistake.script: Я иду на работу пешком каждый день.
mistake.why: L2-M4's idú is the walk you are on right now. Bolted to kázhdyy den' it claims one endless walk to work; a daily habit is khozhú.

sentences.usage: Answering how do you get to work?
sentences.mnemonic: Every day means round trip means indeterminate — khozhú, not idú.

words.note: The indeterminate infinitive. Liking, being able and knowing how are all general, never one trip, so a verb of motion after lyublyú is nearly always this one.

sentences.trap: Anything general takes the indeterminate: I like travelling, I can drive, I go by train. English has no signal for this at all, so the rule has to be applied deliberately.
sentences.sound: YEZ-dit — front-stressed, and the final t is soft, the tongue flat behind the teeth.

variations.changed: the on-foot verb, in the same general slot
a different traveller and a different vehicle

mistake.why: L2-M4's yékhat' is the one-direction verb, so this says you like being on this particular journey. A general fondness for train travel is yézdit'.

sentences.usage: Small talk about how you like to get around.
sentences.mnemonic: A liking is never one trip, so it never takes the determinate.

sentences.display: On poyékhal tudá vcherá i yeshchyó ne vernúlsya.
sentences.script: Он поехал туда вчера и ещё не вернулся.
sentences.cue: He went there yesterday and hasn't come back yet.
sentences.literal: He set-off there yesterday and still not returned.

words.note: po- on the determinate stem, which makes it PERFECTIVE: one departure, and no return promised. The same machine gave L3-M10 its ushyól, prishyól and priyékhal.
There, as a destination — the answer to L2-M4's kudá. L1-M7's tam is where something IS; tudá is where it is going.

sentences.trap: tam and tudá are both there in English and never swap in Russian. Motion takes tudá; standing still takes tam; and the same split runs through zdes' against syudá.
sentences.sound: pa-YE-khal — stress in the middle, the po- unstressed and reduced to pa.

variations.changed: a woman, so the past takes -a
L1-M5's domóy as the destination

mistake.display: On yézdil tudá vcherá i yeshchyó ne vernúlsya.
mistake.script: Он ездил туда вчера и ещё не вернулся.
mistake.why: L3-M10's yézdil already says he went and came back, so the second half of the sentence contradicts the first. If he is still there, the verb has to be the one-way poyékhal.

sentences.usage: Explaining why someone is not around.
sentences.mnemonic: A prefix on the one-way stem makes a one-way perfective: he left, full stop.

sentences.display: Doyédete do stántsii, potóm poverníte nalévo.
sentences.script: Доедете до станции, потом поверните налево.
sentences.cue: Ride as far as the station, then turn left.
sentences.literal: You-will-reach up-to station, then turn left.

words.cue: you ride as far as, you get to
words.note: do- on the determinate stem: travel AS FAR AS a point, and stop there. It answers do plus the genitive, which is L2-M4's frame unchanged.
Turn, said to vy. The stress falls on the ní; L2-M4 printed this word without its acute, and the accent is the only thing that tells a reader where to put the weight.

sentences.trap: Russian gives directions in the future-shaped perfective — doyédete, you will get as far as — where English uses a bare imperative. It is not a prediction; it is how instructions are worded.
sentences.sound: da-YE-di-tye — the do- is unstressed and reduces to da, exactly as po- does in poyékhal.

variations.display: Doyédete do ploshchadi, potóm poverníte naprávo.
variations.script: Доедете до площади, потом поверните направо.
variations.cue: Ride as far as the square, then turn right.
variations.changed: a different landmark and the other turn

variations.cue: You need to ride as far as the stop.
variations.changed: the infinitive under L3-M4's nádo

mistake.display: Doyédete do stántsiya, potóm poverníte nalévo.
mistake.script: Доедете до станция, потом поверните налево.
mistake.why: do has taken the genitive since L2-M4 and has not changed: do stántsii. The nominative stántsiya after it stops the sentence dead for a listener following directions.

sentences.usage: Telling a stranger how to get somewhere by metro or bus.
sentences.mnemonic: do- means up to and no further — the prefix and the preposition say the same thing twice.

sentences.cue: You need to change to a bus.

words.note: Literally to re-sit: pere- across plus sit. It takes na plus the ACCUSATIVE for the line you move onto, because you are moving onto it.

sentences.trap: English change is vague; Russian names the seat. peresést' works for anything you sit down in and never for a plane ticket or a decision, which take different verbs entirely.
sentences.sound: pi-ri-SYEST — stress on the last syllable, and the final t is soft.

variations.cue: You need to change to the metro.
variations.changed: a different line to change onto
the place said and the destination left out

mistake.why: na avtóbuse is the prepositional and means while on a bus — so the sentence has you changing seats inside one. Moving ONTO a service takes the accusative: na avtóbus.

sentences.usage: Answering how do I get there? when it is not one ride.
sentences.mnemonic: You move onto a line, so the line goes in the accusative.

sentences.display: Peresádka na metró, a obrátno mózhno peshkóm.
sentences.script: Пересадка на метро, а обратно можно пешком.
sentences.cue: There's a change onto the metro, and you can walk back.
sentences.literal: Change onto metro, and back possible on-foot.

words.note: The noun for the change itself, printed on signs and said at counters. Built from the same pere- plus sit as peresést', but a separate word rather than one of its forms.
The return leg of a journey — obrátno mózhno peshkóm, you can walk back. It is about the trip, not about direction in space.

sentences.trap: obrátno is the second half of a there-and-back, which is why it sits so naturally beside khodíl and yézdil. It never means backwards, and never describes which way something faces.
sentences.sound: ab-RAT-na — stress in the middle, and both unstressed o's come out as a.

variations.cue: The change to the bus is here.
variations.changed: the noun with a place instead of a second clause
just the return leg, on its own

mistake.display: Peresádka na metró, a nazád mózhno peshkóm.
mistake.script: Пересадка на метро, а назад можно пешком.
mistake.why: nazád is backwards — the direction you face or step. The word for the return half of a journey is obrátno, and swapping them makes the sentence about walking in reverse.

sentences.usage: Working out a route aloud with someone.
sentences.mnemonic: obrátno closes the loop that the indeterminate verbs already draw.

sentences.cue: From here the bus goes as far as the square.

words.note: From here — the third member of the set with L1-M7's zdes', here, and tudá, to there. Russian keeps where, to where and from where apart in every one of them.
The third person of L2-M4's idtí, and it is used of buses and trains as well as people — a route runs the way a person walks, in one direction.

sentences.trap: A bus is transport, so a learner reaches for yédet. Russian says idyót of a scheduled service: the route goes, whatever is carrying you along it.
sentences.sound: i-DYOT — stress on the second syllable, and the yó vowel is always the stressed one, wherever it appears.

variations.cue: From here the train goes as far as Moscow.
variations.changed: a train and a longer route

variations.cue: The bus goes as far as the stop.
variations.changed: no starting point named

mistake.why: Correct, and it says something else: khódit describes the service as a thing that runs regularly. idyót is about the line this bus takes, which is what someone at the stop is asking.

sentences.usage: Reading a route off a stop for someone who cannot.
sentences.mnemonic: A route goes in one direction, so a route takes the determinate.
